gittin-5b-19-20.note: Bar Haddaya wants to carry a divorce document from one country to another and asks how closely he must watch it being written. Rabbi Ahai says he must stand over every letter the scribe writes. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi say it is enough to be present and generally make sure it is done properly. The passage adds that insisting on Ahai's strict way would cast doubt on earlier divorce documents, whose carriers never checked that closely.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: a man carrying a divorce document between countries

people.name: Rabbi Ahai
people.about: appointed over divorce documents in his location

terms.meaning: The formal document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

gittin-5b-21-21.note: Rabba bar bar Chana brought a divorce document half of which was written in his presence and half not. Rabbi Elazar ruled that if the scribe wrote even one line for the woman in his presence, the rest is assumed to be written for her too. Rav Ashi adds that even hearing the sound of the quill and the scroll while it was being written is enough.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives to end a marriage; it must be written specifically for that woman.

gittin-6a-18-18.note: Rav Hanin recalls that Rav Kahana brought a divorce document between Sura and Neharde'a, two Babylonian cities, but does not remember which direction. Rav Kahana asked Rav whether he must declare that it was written and signed in his presence. Rav answered that he does not have to.

terms.term: declaration 'written and signed in my presence'
terms.meaning: A statement an agent bringing a divorce document from abroad makes to confirm it was properly written and signed.

gittin-6b-1-3.note: A man bringing a divorce document asks Rabbi Yishmael whether he must say it was written and signed in his presence. Learning he is from the village of Sisai, Rabbi Yishmael tells him he must say it, so the woman will not need witnesses if her husband disputes it. Rabbi Elai objects that Sisai is inside the Land of Israel, where the declaration is not required. Rabbi Yishmael tells him to be quiet: once the divorce was given on the basis of the declaration, it is valid, showing the declaration protects the divorce from later challenge.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: a student who questions the ruling

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings closely related to the Mishnah.

gittin-6b-11-12.note: Rabbi Evyatar asks Elijah the prophet what God is doing, and Elijah says God is studying the story of the concubine in Gibeah and quoting Evyatar's view and Yonatan's differing view. Evyatar wonders why God would mention two opinions if He knows what happened. Elijah answers that both opinions are the words of the living God, and explains how both could be true: the man found a fly in his food and was not upset, but later found a hair and was.

terms.meaning: A disturbing biblical story from the Book of Judges about a man and his concubine.

gittin-7a-1-2.note: Rabbi Abbahu teaches that a person should not frighten his household too much, since a great man did and they nearly gave him forbidden food. It was Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel. The Gemara says he did not actually eat forbidden food: when the animal they brought was missing a limb, his frightened household cut one from a live animal to make it look whole, and he almost ate it.

terms.meaning: A limb cut from a living animal, which the Torah forbids eating.

gittin-7a-4-6.note: Mar Ukva, leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia, writes to Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel asking whether he may hand over men who torment him to the government. Rabbi Elazar replies only with Bible verses telling him to hold his tongue. When Mar Ukva writes again, Rabbi Elazar tells him to wait patiently for God and to go to the study hall earlier and leave later than his tormentors, and they will disappear on their own. As soon as Rabbi Elazar said this, Geneiva, Mar Ukva's tormentor, was put in a neck iron as a government prisoner.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: the Exilarch, leader of the Jews in Babylonia

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, recognized by the government.
Draw lines on parchment before writing, as a scribe does.

gittin-7a-12-15.note: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna where the ban on placing a garland on a groom's head comes from. Rav Huna cites a mishnah: during Vespasian's war the Sages banned wedding garlands and drums. While Rav Huna steps out, his student Rav Hisda offers a verse (Ezekiel 21:31): when the High Priest's mitre was in place, everyone could wear a garland, and when it is removed, so is the garland. Rav Huna returns and says the ban is rabbinic, but praises Hisda for finding a fine source.

terms.meaning: The headdress of the High Priest in the Temple.
A rule instituted by the Sages rather than stated in the Torah.

gittin-7a-16-16.note: Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a wedding garland for his daughter and asks if he doesn't follow the rule against garlands derived from the verse about the mitre being removed. Mar bar Rav Ashi answers that the ban applies to men, those comparable to a High Priest. The Sages did not extend it to women, so he may make the garland.

terms.meaning: A rule the Sages enacted as a safeguard or response to events.

gittin-11b-9-11.note: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef discuss whether someone who grabs property for a creditor acquires it for him, while Rabbi Yirmeya dozes nearby. He wakes up and corrects them: if the grab harms other creditors, it does not count. The case of the slave's divorce-from-ownership document is different, because the master said 'give' it, which the Talmud treats like 'acquire it for him'.

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.
The earlier collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.

gittin-14a-8-10.note: Gardeners settled accounts and one was told to give the leftover five coins to the landowner, who formally acquired the money in front of everyone. The gardener later recalculated and found he had no surplus, and asked Rav Nahman for help. Rav Nahman first says he can do nothing, since the landowner already acquired the money. After Rava points out the gardener never said he would not pay a real debt, only that the money was not in his possession, Rav Nahman agrees it was an acquisition made in error, which reverts to the previous owner.

terms.meaning: A formal act that makes a transfer of ownership legally binding.
A unit of money of the time.

gittin-14a-16-17.note: Rav Sheshet had cloaks with merchants in Mehoza and asked Rav Yosef bar Hama to bring back the money. The merchants who handed it over wanted a formal act of acquisition so Yosef would be responsible if anything happened to it. Yosef said yes but slipped away without doing it. Rav Sheshet told him he did well, citing the verse 'the borrower is a slave to the lender': either because Yosef avoided binding himself for no reason, or, in another version, because the merchants who owed Sheshet had to see that the money reached him.

terms.meaning: A formal act that makes someone legally responsible for an item or sum.

gittin-14a-18-18.note: Rabbi Achai asks two men to fetch a silver vessel from Neharde'a. The holders hand it over but ask for a formal act making the carriers responsible on the way; the carriers refuse, and the holders want it back. Rabbi Yosei refuses to return it, is roughed up, and Rabbi Dostai says 'hit him'. Rabbi Dostai later explains the holders were frightening men who might have killed him.

terms.meaning: A formal act that makes a transfer or a responsibility legally binding.

gittin-14b-17-17.note: Rabbi Elazar's colleagues cite a case of a sick woman of the Rokhel family who said to give her brooch, worth 1,200 dinars, to her daughter. After she died, the Sages carried out her wish. Rabbi Elazar curses her sons, meaning it is no proof: they were wicked, so the Sages bent the usual inheritance rules there.

terms.meaning: A coin used as a unit of money.

gittin-16b-14-14.note: Rabba bar bar Chana is sick, and Rav Yehuda and Rabba visit him. He answers their question: two people bringing a divorce document from overseas need not say it was written and signed in their presence. Then a Persian priest takes their lamp on a Persian holiday, and Rabba prays to live under either God's shadow or the Romans, not under the Persians.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: from the Land of Israel, per the text

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-18b-6-6.note: A man told ten men to write a divorce document for his wife. Two signed that day and the others up to ten days later. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that Rabbi Shimon's view, which allows a document written by day and signed at night, can be relied on in urgent circumstances, so once given, the woman is divorced.

terms.meaning: An urgent situation where the rabbis allow a more lenient ruling.

gittin-19a-16-16.note: A man had witnesses trace their names in ink on documents that were not divorce documents. Rav Kahana ordered him flogged for doing so. The text does not explain the reason, but it is told in a discussion of a method of tracing signatures that is sometimes allowed on divorce documents.

terms.meaning: Having witnesses go over a name already written, rather than writing it themselves.
A punishment of lashes ordered by a court.

gittin-19b-18-18.note: A man threw what he said was a divorce document into his wife's courtyard among the barrels, but only a mezuza was found there. The question is whether the document was lost and a mezuza happened to be there, or whether he really threw a mezuza and only called it a divorce document. Rav Nahman says a mezuza is rarely kept among barrels, so we assume he threw the mezuza, not a divorce document.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses, fixed to a doorpost.
The formal document that ends a marriage.

gittin-19b-20-20.note: A man took a Torah scroll in the synagogue, gave it to his wife, and said 'This is your bill of divorce.' Rav Yosef considers whether he might have secretly written the divorce on the scroll in invisible gall-water ink. He says that cannot be, since the parchment is itself treated with gall water and a second layer would not last, so there is no concern that a divorce document was written there.

terms.meaning: A liquid used to treat parchment and make ink; here, an invisible way of writing.

gittin-27a-4-5.note: Rabba is said to contradict himself. A divorce document turned up in Rav Huna's court naming 'Sheviri the city, on the Rakhis River', and Rav Huna worried there might be two cities of that name, so it might belong to another man. Rav Hisda told Rabba, then a student, to study the issue before Rav Huna questioned him that night. Rabba found a mishnah saying court-authenticated notes are returned to their owner with no worry about two towns of the same name.

terms.meaning: Documents, such as promissory notes, that a court has authenticated.

gittin-27b-8-8.note: Rabba bar bar Hana lost a divorce document he was carrying in the study hall, and said he could identify it by a distinguishing mark or by sight. They returned it to him. Afterward he admitted he did not know whether it was returned because of the mark, which Torah law may accept for lost items, or because Torah scholars like him are trusted to recognize an item, which an ordinary man would not be.

terms.meaning: A feature by which an owner can identify a lost item and reclaim it.

gittin-29b-8-9.note: A husband sent a divorce document with an agent who did not know the wife, and told him to give it to Abba bar Minyumi, who does. Not finding Abba bar Minyumi, the agent asked three Sages, who said he should hand his agency over to them so they could pass it to Abba bar Minyumi. Rav Safra, sitting with them, objected that the agent was only authorized to hand it to Abba bar Minyumi and cannot pass the role to others. The three Sages were embarrassed that they had ruled wrongly.

terms.meaning: Someone appointed to deliver a divorce document for the husband.

gittin-29b-12-16.note: A husband told his agent not to deliver a divorce document until thirty days passed, but circumstances beyond the agent's control meant he could not wait. Rava had him transfer his agency to Rava's court, which would appoint a new agent after thirty days. The Sages challenged this twice, and the second challenge, about the husband changing his mind, seemed to go unanswered; Rava was embarrassed. Then it came out that the woman was only betrothed, not married, and Rava said a man is less likely to change his mind about such a woman, so his ruling was correct.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: quotes a teaching of Rav Huna in Rav's name

terms.meaning: Engaged under a formal betrothal, but not yet fully married.

gittin-30a-1-1.note: A man gave agents a divorce document, saying it would take effect if he had not arrived within thirty days. He reached the river at the end of day thirty, but the ferry was on the far side, so he shouted that he had arrived. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as arriving, even though he clearly meant to, so the divorce document is valid.

terms.meaning: A divorce document that takes effect only if a stated condition is, or is not, met.

gittin-30a-2-2.note: A man left a divorce document with agents, saying it would take effect if he did not appease his wife within thirty days. He went to appease her, but she was not appeased. Rav Yosef said that he did not truly meet his condition, since he did not even give her a large vessel full of dinars, so the divorce document is valid.

terms.meaning: Win her over so that she is no longer upset with him.

gittin-31b-9-10.note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda see Geneiva passing, and one wants to stand for him as a son of the Torah, but the other says he is quarrelsome. Geneiva then asks what they were discussing and they say winds. He passes on a teaching from Rav: four winds blow each day, with the north wind always among them, as the world could not survive without it. The south wind is harshest and would destroy the world were it not held back by the angel Ben Netz.

terms.meaning: An angel said here to hold back the south wind; the name echoes 'netz' (hawk) in Job 39:26.

gittin-31b-11-13.note: Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak see Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov riding past in a gilded carriage with a green cloak. Rava goes to him; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak first holds back, then also goes when he sees who it is. Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov bares his arm in the heat and names the Shadya wind, and they report Rav, Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan on its harmful effects on pregnancy and pearls. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak then shows that all three sayings come from one verse in Hosea (13:15).

terms.meaning: The name of a harmful wind in this passage.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

gittin-33b-11-11.note: Rabba bar bar Hana remembers five elders sitting before Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha when a man was pressed, against his will, to authorize a divorce document. Rabbi Yoshiya told the elders to go hide while they wrote it, so the husband could not find them and cancel it after it was written. The passage is used to show that Rabbi Yoshiya followed a particular legal view.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: tells the story as an eyewitness

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife to end a Jewish marriage.

gittin-34a-2-3.note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a divorce document to his wife, but she delayed the messenger by asking him to come back tomorrow. When Giddul heard, he said a blessing thanking God, because he was glad the divorce had not been delivered. The Sages then disagreed: Abaye said his words do not cancel the divorce, while Rava said they do.

terms.meaning: A messenger the husband sends to hand the divorce document to his wife.
Legally cancelled, so it no longer counts as a valid divorce.

gittin-34a-5-5.note: Rava points to a case where Rav Sheshet pressed a man to authorize a divorce document against his will. The man then told the witnesses that Rav Sheshet had really said to cancel it. Rav Sheshet made him authorize a new document, which shows he treated the first one as cancelled, even though the man never said so outright.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
Legally cancelled.

gittin-34a-7-7.note: Abaye tells of Rav Yehuda pressing the son-in-law of Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a to authorize a divorce document. The man cancelled it, twice. The third time Rav Yehuda forced it against his will and had the witnesses put gourd pieces in their ears so they would not hear any cancellation. Abaye argues that if a disclosure of intent mattered in divorce, the document would be void, since the witnesses could see him running after them even without hearing him. So such disclosures must be disregarded.

terms.meaning: A person's stated private feeling or wish, which the Talmud asks whether it can change a legal act.

gittin-34a-11-11.note: A man gave his betrothed a divorce document and told the witnesses it would count as a divorce if he did not marry her within thirty days. When the thirty days ended, he told them he had tried but failed to marry her. The passage as given does not state the ruling.

terms.meaning: A woman who is engaged in the formal Jewish sense, which already needs a divorce to end.

gittin-35a-1-2.note: The Gemara asks why courts stopped making widows take oaths, and considers whether the reason is a story told by Rav Kahana (or, some say, by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav). During a famine, a man left a gold coin with a widow. Without knowing it, she baked the coin into bread and gave the bread to a poor man. When the owner asked for the coin, she swore that one of her children should be poisoned if she had benefited from it, and soon one of her children died. The Sages concluded that if even a truthful oath is punished this way, a false oath is punished all the more. The Gemara offers this only as a possible reason for the practice.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: one of two possible sources of the story (others say Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav)

terms.meaning: Left with someone for safekeeping, so the keeper must return it.

gittin-35a-10-10.note: A widow asked Rav Huna to collect her marriage contract payment from her dead husband's orphaned children. He said he could not help her, because Rav does not let a widow collect it. She replied that the only reason was the concern that she had already taken some of it, and she swore on the spot by the Lord of Hosts that she had not benefited from it at all. Rav Huna ruled that although the court does not make a widow swear, Rav agrees that when she swears of her own accord the oath is accepted, so she can collect.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Huna's teacher, whose ruling he quotes

terms.meaning: A written promise of money the husband owes his wife, due when the marriage ends by divorce or his death.
Here, the dead husband's children, who inherit his property and would have to pay.

gittin-35a-10-13.note: This passage holds two cases. First, a widow volunteers an oath before Rav Huna and is allowed to collect her marriage contract. Then another widow comes to Rabba bar Rav Huna, who refuses both her marriage contract and her living expenses, citing his father and Shmuel. She curses him; he turns his chair over to fulfil the curse in a small way, but is still left weakened.

terms.meaning: A written promise of money the husband owes his wife, due when the marriage ends by divorce or his death.
Support for a widow's living costs paid from her late husband's property, until she remarries.

gittin-36a-2-2.note: A teacher of children was banned from teaching by a public vow, because he hit the children too much. Later the vow was cancelled and he was reinstated, since no other teacher as careful could be found. The Gemara uses this to show that a vow can be undone when it is needed for a mitzva (a religious duty), such as teaching children.

people.name: Rav Aḥa
people.about: put the teacher under the vow

terms.meaning: A legal process by which a rabbinic authority cancels a vow someone has taken.
A commandment or religious duty.

gittin-37a-10-12.note: Rabbi Asi's relative held a loan document with a property guarantee and asked Rabbi Asi whether the Sabbatical Year cancels the debt. Rabbi Asi said no, but Rabbi Yohanan told the relative that it does. When Rabbi Asi asked him, Rabbi Yohanan again said it does. Rabbi Asi pointed out that Yohanan himself had taught the opposite. Yohanan replied that a view held in theory need not be acted on. When Asi cited a baraita supporting that view, Yohanan suggested it might follow Beit Shammai, whose view on this is not the law.

people.name: Beit Shammai
people.about: a school of scholars whose views usually lose to Beit Hillel

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when private debts are cancelled.
A written document recording a loan.
A teaching from the time of the Mishna that is not in the Mishna itself.

gittin-37b-2-3.note: Abba bar Marta brought money to repay Rabba during the Sabbatical Year, when debts are cancelled. Rabba said he cancelled the debt, and Abba took him literally and left with the money. Abaye told him to go back and say he wanted to repay anyway, and then Rabba accepted it. Rabba remarked that this Torah scholar had not known how to respond and had to be taught.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: got Abba bar Marta to go back

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when private debts are cancelled.

gittin-38a-9-10.note: Shmuel's maidservant was captured and some people redeemed her, then sent her back to him as a maidservant. They claimed even the Rabbis would agree she stayed his. Shmuel did not treat her as a slave and did not even require a document of freedom, since he held she was fully free. The passage says he had already given up hope of getting her back.

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
Giving up hope of recovering something lost, which ends the owner's claim to it.

gittin-38a-12-12.note: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant was captured, and a non-Jew from Palmyra (a tarmoda'a) redeemed her to be his wife. The Sages sent Rabbi Abba a message that if he wanted to act correctly, he should send her a document of freedom. The text gives only this advice, not the reason or what happened next.

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A word the text applies to the gentile who redeemed her; its exact meaning is not explained here.

gittin-38a-16-16.note: In Pumbedita, people were having forbidden sexual relations with a certain maidservant, and her master could not stop it. Abaye said he would force the master to free her, so she could marry a Jew and the forbidden conduct would end, except that Rav Yehuda, quoting Shmuel, says freeing a slave breaks a commandment. Ravina replied that in such a case Rav Yehuda would agree that freeing her is allowed, because of the sin others are committing.

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A commandment to do something, as opposed to a prohibition.

gittin-38a-16-17.note: A maidservant in Pumbedita was being abused by men, and her master could not stop it. Abaye says he would force the master to free her, were it not that freeing a slave is generally forbidden. Ravina says freeing her is allowed here. The Gemara cites a case where the court forced a master to free a half-free woman because men took liberties with her.

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.

gittin-38b-3-3.note: Rabbi Eliezer went into a synagogue to pray and found only nine men, so he freed his slave to complete the group of ten needed for communal prayer. This is raised as an objection to the idea that freeing a slave is forbidden. The Gemara answers that freeing a slave for a mitzva, like completing a quorum, is a special case, and does not show it is allowed in general.

terms.meaning: The minimum group of ten adult men needed for certain communal prayers.
A teaching from the time of the Mishna that is not in the Mishna itself.

gittin-39b-13-14.note: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asks where the law stands on Rabbi Shimon's view, and gets conflicting reports. He travels to Sura to learn the actual case: a dying master threw his hat to his crying maidservant and told her to acquire it and thereby acquire herself as free. They went to Rav Naḥman for a ruling, and he said the master had done nothing, meaning she was not freed.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: gave the ruling in the incident

terms.meaning: The accepted Jewish law on a question.

gittin-40a-12-12.note: A city of slaves was sold to gentiles, and after their last owners died the slaves asked Ravina to be treated as fully Jewish. He told them to get freedom documents from their first masters' children. The Rabbis objected, citing Ameimar, but Ravina relied on Rav Dimi's report that the heirs can do this. The Gemara concludes the law follows Ravina.

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.

gittin-40a-14-15.note: A slave had two owners, and one freed his half. The other owner feared the court would force him to free his half too, so he gave the slave to his young son, whom the court cannot force. Rav Pappa replied that, since this was a trick, answer it with one: have the slave jingle coins in front of the child so he agrees to free him, and then write the document.

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.

gittin-43b-4-4.note: Rav Huna bar Ketina quotes a case where a master was forced to free a woman who was half slave, half free. The Gemara asks whether this follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who says women are also commanded to have children. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers no: she was forced to be freed because she could not marry and men were taking liberties with her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two masters and freed by only one, so she is partly free.

gittin-45a-4-4.note: A slave ran away from outside the Land of Israel into it, and his master followed and came to Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Ami told the master to take a written debt for the slave's value and sign a document freeing him. If he refused, Rabbi Ami said he would take the slave from him entirely, since the slave need not go back outside the Land.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A written document recording a debt.
The Land of Israel.

gittin-45a-9-9.note: Rav Ḥisda's slave escaped to a Samaritan village, and the villagers refused to return him, citing a verse that says not to hand a slave back to his master. Rav Ḥisda cited the law of returning lost items, and they repeated their verse. He replied that their verse is about a slave who flees from outside the Land of Israel into it, whereas his slave ran from one place outside the Land to another. The passage ends there.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: his explanation of the verse is cited

terms.meaning: A place where Samaritans lived.
The Land of Israel.

gittin-45a-11-11.note: Abaye lost a donkey among the Samaritans in Bei Kutai and asked for it back. They asked for a identifying sign, and he said its belly was white. They answered that this is not a real sign, since all donkeys have white bellies, but they would send it only because they knew Abaye was trustworthy.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: also called Naḥmani in the text

terms.meaning: A detail that proves a lost item is really yours.
A place where Samaritans lived.

gittin-45a-17-21.note: Rav Naḥman's daughters could stir a boiling pot with bare hands, and were taken captive, along with Rav Ilish, because of the evil eye. A dove's cry convinced Rav Ilish that a miracle would help him escape. He first listened in on the daughters and heard them say they preferred their captors over their real husbands, so he left without them. He escaped across a river, but the bird-language interpreter was caught and killed. After the daughters were later returned, Rav Ilish declared that their pot-stirring had been witchcraft, not righteousness.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: his daughters are the other captives

terms.meaning: A belief that envy or too much attention can bring harm to a person.
Being held by captors, here by a foreign army or raiders.

gittin-45b-11-11.note: An Arab woman merchant brought a sack of tefillin (phylacteries, small boxes with verses worn in prayer) to Abaye. He offered one date for each pair, and in anger she threw them all into the river. Abaye then regretted it, saying he should have offered their actual value instead of speaking of them with such disrespect.

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the head and arm during morning prayer.

gittin-45b-14-14.note: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, reports a case in Tzaidan where a man told his wife he was taking a konam vow, a vow that forbids something as if it were a sacrifice, if he did not divorce her, and he then divorced her. The Sages permitted him to marry her again, for the betterment of the world, meaning a ruling made to keep the social order working.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda

terms.meaning: A form of vow that makes something forbidden to a person as if it were a sacrifice.

terms.term: for the betterment of the world
terms.meaning: A phrase for a rabbinic ruling made to keep the social order working.

gittin-46b-15-16.note: People from Bei Mikhsi borrowed from non-Jews, could not pay, and were seized as slaves. They asked Rav Huna to have fellow Jews redeem them, but he cited a mishna that one who sells himself to non-Jews is not redeemed. Rabbi Abba said that applies only after a repeated third time, but Rav Huna answered that these people do this habitually, so it counts as repeated. The text shows Rav Huna refusing the redemption.

terms.meaning: To pay to free someone held as a slave or captive.

gittin-46b-17-17.note: A man sold himself to gladiators and asked Rabbi Ami to redeem him. Rabbi Ami said that this should be done, since his life was at risk. The Sages said he was an apostate who ate forbidden meat. The man claimed it was only appetite, but they said he skipped permitted food for forbidden food, so Rabbi Ami told him he could not redeem him.

terms.meaning: Animals with an injury that will kill them within a year, which are forbidden to eat.
A Jew who has abandoned the religion.

gittin-47a-3-5.note: Reish Lakish sold himself to gladiators, bringing a bag with a round stone inside. He used a custom that captors grant a condemned man's last wish, asking to tie them up and strike each one. His blows killed them all and he escaped. At home, he lived without worry, saying his belly was his pillow, and left only a small measure of saffron when he died.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: a famous Talmudic sage, also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish

terms.meaning: Fighters who performed in arenas, here those who bought him.
A small unit of volume.

gittin-52a-12-12.note: A steward in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood was selling orphans' land to buy slaves, and Rabbi Meir did not let him. In a dream Meir was shown the words 'I wish to destroy and you build?', which could mean God wanted the orphans to lose their property. Meir ignored it, saying that words seen in dreams neither raise up nor bring down and should not be relied on.

terms.meaning: A person put in charge of an orphan's property until the child grows up.

gittin-52a-13-13.note: Two men, stirred up by Satan, argued every Friday at twilight. Rabbi Meir came by and stopped them three Fridays in a row until he made peace between them. He then heard Satan cry out 'Woe, Rabbi Meir has thrown me out of his house', which shows that Satan lives where there is discord.

terms.meaning: In the Talmud, a figure who tempts and stirs up trouble among people.

gittin-52a-14-14.note: A steward of orphans near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sold their land and bought oxen, and Rabbi Yehoshua said nothing against it. The Gemara explains that he agrees with Rabbi Yosei, who called his ox 'my field' because the ox is what makes a field productive. So buying oxen to work the land counts like keeping the land itself, and there was nothing to protest.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Said he never called his wife 'my wife' but 'my home', and his ox 'my field'.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

gittin-52a-15-17.note: An old woman who cared for some orphans sold their ox, and their relatives objected to Rav Nachman. He first said that living with the orphans gave her the authority of a steward, and that a price rise after the sale was the buyer's gain, not the orphans' loss. But when the relatives pointed out that the money had not yet been paid, he agreed: orphans' property is only fully sold once money is handed over, so the orphans can raise the price or cancel the sale.

people.name: Rav Nachman
people.about: A Babylonian sage who judged this case.

people.name: Rav Chanilai bar Idi
people.about: Quoted as passing on a teaching of Shmuel.

terms.meaning: Property dedicated to the Temple, which can only be sold properly by actual payment; orphans' property is treated the same way.

gittin-52a-18-18.note: Buyers agreed to buy the orphan Rabbana Ukva's wine at four dinars a barrel and took hold of it, but the price rose to six before they paid. Rav Nachman ruled that, because orphans' property is only fully acquired when money changes hands, the buyers must pay the higher price or the sale is cancelled.

people.name: Rabbana Ukva
people.about: An orphan who owned the wine.

terms.meaning: A silver coin used as money.

gittin-52b-4-5.note: Orphans' relatives complained to Rav Nachman that the steward Amram the dyer dressed well and ate lavishly on the orphans' money. Rav Nachman gave innocent explanations each time: fine clothes help him be taken seriously, and perhaps he found a lost item. When they said he was actually damaging the property, Rav Nachman said to bring witnesses and he would remove him, and the Gemara concludes that a court does remove a steward who damages orphans' property.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reported a ruling in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the accepted ruling.

gittin-54a-5-5.note: Someone insulted another man by calling him a convert and the son of a convert. The man snapped back that at least he did not eat produce of the Sabbatical Year, as the insulter did. The Gemara uses this as proof that people in that place treated the Sabbatical Year ban as a serious matter, which is why Rabbi Yehuda did not impose a penalty for unintentional breaking of it.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when the land in Israel is left to rest and its produce is not sold or eaten in the usual way.
Someone who was not born Jewish but joined the Jewish people.

gittin-54b-9-9.note: A man told his partner that food they had prepared together in a state of ritual purity had become impure. The owner asked Rabbi Ami, who said he could keep treating the food as pure, since the other man is not believed. Rabbi Asi objected that Rabbi Yochanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei, said the Torah does treat such a person as believable. The passage ends there with the two views side by side.

terms.meaning: A status in Jewish law that affects whether food and objects may be used in holy settings or eaten in a state of purity.

gittin-54b-13-14.note: A scribe told Rabbi Ami that he had not written God's names with the proper intention in a Torah scroll he made for a buyer, which would make it invalid. Rabbi Ami ruled that he is believed enough to lose his payment, but not believed enough to disqualify the scroll the buyer holds. Rabbi Yirmeya asked whether he loses payment for the whole scroll or just the God's names; Rabbi Ami said the whole scroll, since a scroll with those names written wrongly is worth nothing.

terms.meaning: The requirement that a scribe have in mind that he is writing a holy name when he writes it.

gittin-54b-18-18.note: A scribe told Rabbi Abbahu that he had not prepared the parchment of a Torah scroll he sold with the proper holy intention. Rabbi Abbahu asked who held the scroll now, and learned the buyer did. He ruled that since the scribe is believed enough to lose his payment, he is also believed enough to disqualify the scroll.

terms.meaning: The animal skin used for a Torah scroll has to be prepared with the specific purpose of making a holy scroll.

gittin-55b-6-6.note: Rava objects, using a mishna and a baraita (an early teaching outside the mishna), that a thief who consecrates a stolen animal is still liable for karet, a severe heavenly punishment. That seems to need the thief to own it. Rav Sheizevi's answer made people laugh, but Rava defends it: the Sages themselves made the thief's consecration valid, so the animal counts as his.

terms.meaning: A severe punishment of being cut off from the Jewish people, imposed by Heaven.
To set an animal aside as holy, as an offering.
An early teaching not included in the Mishna.

gittin-55b-15-17.note: Rabbi Yochanan says Jerusalem fell because of Kamtza and bar Kamtza. A host mistakenly invited his enemy bar Kamtza to a feast and threw him out despite offers to pay. Angry that the Sages stayed silent, bar Kamtza told the Roman emperor the Jews were rebelling, and tricked them by blemishing an offering he brought. Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas blocked every fix the Sages proposed, and the war with Rome began.

terms.meaning: A physical defect that makes an animal unfit to be offered on the altar.
The central holy building in Jerusalem, where offerings were brought.

gittin-56a-5-6.note: Rome sent Nero against the Jews. He shot arrows in all four directions and each one landed in Jerusalem. Then he asked a child to recite a verse he had learned, and it was 'I will lay My vengeance upon Edom by the hand of My people Israel'. Nero concluded that God wanted to destroy the Temple and then punish him for it, so he fled and became a convert, and Rabbi Meir was said to be his descendant.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Said here to descend from Nero.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Esau; the Talmud uses it as a name for Rome.

gittin-56a-7-9.note: Vespasian besieged Jerusalem for three years. Three rich men, Nakdimon ben Guryon, ben Kalba Savua and ben Tzitzit HaKesat, offered food, drink and firewood, enough for twenty-one years. The Sages wanted to make peace with Rome, but the zealots refused and wanted to fight. To force the issue, the zealots burned the storehouses of wheat and barley, and a famine followed.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: One of three wealthy men of Jerusalem.

people.name: Rav Chisda
people.about: Quoted on how costly firewood is.

terms.meaning: Hardline fighters in besieged Jerusalem who opposed making peace with Rome.

gittin-56a-10-13.note: During the famine, the rich woman Marta bat Baitos sent her agent for flour, but each kind (fine, ordinary, coarse, even barley) was sold out before he got there. She went out to look for food herself, stepped on dung, and died of disgust. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai applied to her a verse about a tender and delicate woman. Another version says she died of disgust after eating a fig that Rabbi Tzadok had sucked dry. He ate figs this way while breaking the fasts he kept for forty years, praying that Jerusalem would not be destroyed. It is also told that as she was dying she threw her gold and silver into the marketplace, saying she had no use for it, which the Gemara links to a verse in Ezekiel.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Fasted forty years, praying Jerusalem would not be destroyed.

terms.meaning: Fine flour, the best kind.

gittin-56a-14-17.note: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked his nephew Abba Sikkara, leader of the zealots, to help him leave Jerusalem. Abba Sikkara told him to pretend to be sick and then dead, and had his students carry him out in a coffin. The guards wanted to stab or push the body to check, but Abba Sikkara talked them out of it, and the gate was opened. Reaching the Roman camp, Yochanan greeted Vespasian as king, and Vespasian replied that he deserved death twice over.

people.name: Abba Sikkara
people.about: Leader of the zealots and nephew of Yochanan ben Zakkai.

gittin-56b-7-16.note: Titus conquered the Temple, brought a prostitute into the Holy of Holies, did a shameful act on a Torah scroll, and slashed the curtain, which poured out blood. He also loaded the sacred vessels onto a ship to be praised in his city for conquering Jerusalem. At sea a wave nearly drowned him, and he boasted that God only had power over water. A heavenly voice dared him to go up on dry land and fight a gnat; when he did, a gnat entered his nose and ate at his brain for seven years. Hammering eased it for thirty days. When he was dying he ordered that he be burned and his ashes scattered across the seven seas so God could not find him and judge him. After his death his head was opened and the gnat was found to be the size of a sparrow.

people.name: Titus
people.about: Roman commander who took Jerusalem; son of Vespasian.

people.name: Rabbi Pinchas ben Arova
people.about: Said he was in Rome when Titus died and saw the gnat.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, once a year.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

gittin-56b-17-17.note: Onkelos, Titus's nephew, wants to convert to Judaism. He raises Titus from the grave and asks who is most important in the next world. Titus says the Jewish people, and advises Onkelos to fight against them rather than join them, since their commandments are too many. Onkelos asks Titus what his punishment is, and Titus answers: every day his ashes are gathered, judged and burned, and scattered over the seven seas.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
people.about: Titus's nephew (his sister's son), who wants to convert

people.name: Titus
people.about: the Roman who destroyed the Temple, raised from the grave

terms.meaning: Calling up the dead to ask them questions.

gittin-57a-4-8.note: Rabbi Elazar says the story of bar Kamtza shows the power of shame. Then the Gemara tells how King's Mountain fell. Roman soldiers took the rooster and hen carried before a wedding procession, the townspeople beat them, and the emperor came to war. A local man, bar Deroma, who could leap a mil, killed many Romans. But he spoke a verse against God as a statement of fact, and he died when a snake tore him open in an outhouse. The emperor spared the rest. The Jews then celebrated with so many candles that a seal's image could be seen a mil away, and the emperor, thinking they were rejoicing over him, came back against them.

people.name: Bar Deroma
people.about: A man who could leap a mil and killed many Romans.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly two-thirds of a mile or about a kilometer.

gittin-57a-14-15.note: A betrothed couple were captured by non-Jews, who married them to each other. The woman asked the man not to touch her because she had no marriage contract from him, and he never did until he died. She then asked the Sages to eulogize him as having mastered his desire even more than Joseph, since Joseph only resisted briefly, was not in the same bed, and the woman was not his wife.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical Joseph, who resisted Potiphar's wife.

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband commits to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

gittin-57a-17-18.note: A husband wanted to divorce his wife without paying her large marriage contract. He got his friends drunk, put them in bed with her, smeared egg white to look like evidence, and brought witnesses to court claiming adultery. Bava ben Buta, a student of Shammai, said that egg white hardens near fire while semen is absorbed. They tested it, found egg white, and punished the husband with lashes and made him pay her contract in full.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: A disciple of Shammai the Elder.

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband commits to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

gittin-57b-11-12.note: Four hundred boys and girls were taken captive to be used for prostitution. They asked whether drowning themselves in the sea would still bring them to the World-to-Come, and the eldest cited a verse that God will bring back those who drown for Heaven's sake. The girls jumped into the sea, and the boys reasoned that if the girls would do it, they should too, and followed. The passage applies the verse about being killed all day long to them.

terms.meaning: The afterlife, where the righteous receive their reward.

gittin-57b-13-19.note: A woman's seven sons were brought one by one before the emperor and told to worship an idol. Each refused, quoting a Torah verse, and each was killed. The youngest was offered a trick to save his life, dropping the emperor's seal and picking it up, but he refused too, saying that if he should honor Caesar, he must all the more honor God. His mother kissed him goodbye, said she had bound seven altars, then fell from a roof and died. A heavenly voice called her a joyful mother of children.

people.name: The mother and her seven sons
Abraham
people.about: Whom the mother mentions, since he bound one son (Isaac) on an altar.

terms.meaning: Dying rather than break the Torah's core commandments, as a witness to God.

gittin-58a-5-5.note: The Gemara describes the cruel treatment of handsome Jewish children by Roman nobles after the Great Revolt. In one case two of the children talk. One asks where such suffering appears in the Torah, and the other cites a verse about plagues not written in the Torah. When the first asks how far off in his studies that verse was, his friend says one and a half columns. He answers that he would not have needed him.

terms.meaning: The Jewish war against Rome that ended with the destruction of the Temple.

gittin-58a-7-7.note: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel, who quotes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, to explain a verse from Lamentations. The city of Beitar had four hundred synagogues, each with four hundred teachers and four hundred pupils. When the enemy broke in, the children attacked with their pens. After the enemy won, they wrapped the children in their scrolls and burned them.

gittin-58a-8-9.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya came to Rome and heard of a handsome child in prison. Standing outside, he quoted a verse about Israel being given to robbers, and the child finished it correctly, with the reason, that we sinned against God. Rabbi Yehoshua was sure the child would become a great teacher and swore not to leave until he ransomed him. He paid a great sum, and soon the child was giving legal rulings in Israel. He was Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

terms.meaning: Decisions on what Jewish law requires.

gittin-58a-10-12.note: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest were captured and sold to two different masters. The masters decided to pair the two beautiful slaves and share the children, and locked them in a room. Each sat in a corner and wept, unwilling to marry a slave given their priestly descent. At dawn they recognized each other as brother and sister and died of grief, and the passage connects their fate with Jeremiah's lament.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: Called the High Priest here; his son and daughter are the subjects.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports this in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, with special status and marriage restrictions.

gittin-58a-13-15.note: Reish Lakish tells of Tzafenat bat Peniel, a High Priest's daughter known for her beauty. After she was captured and abused, she was put up for sale in seven garments, and an ugly man insisted on seeing her beauty. Six garments were removed, and she tore the seventh herself and rolled in ashes. She cried out to God, asking why He had not shown pity at least for the sake of His own holy name by which they are called.

people.name: Tzafenat bat Peniel
people.about: A High Priest's daughter known for her beauty.

gittin-58a-17-20.note: A carpenter's apprentice wanted his master's wife. He kept her for three days when she came to get a loan, then falsely told the master she had been attacked on the way back. He persuaded the master to divorce her, lent him money for her marriage contract, and married her himself. When the master could not repay, the apprentice made him work it off, serving the couple their drinks with tears falling into the cups. The Gemara says Israel's sentence was sealed for staying silent about this, though some say it was for the couple's earlier adultery.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports this in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband commits to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

gittin-58b-9-10.note: Giddel bar Re'ilai took over absent neighbors' land in a valley by paying their land tax, and paid three years in advance. After one year the original owners came back, said he had already eaten that year's produce, and wanted the land back. Rav Pappa first considered letting Giddel hold the land two more years to cover his outlay. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objected that this follows the law of the Sicarii, which does not apply in Babylonia, and said Giddel had risked his own money, so it counts as a gift. The passage does not say whether Rav Pappa accepted this.

people.name: Giddel bar Re'ilai
people.about: Paid the land tax in advance.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua

terms.meaning: A name for violent seizers of land, and for a legal rule about buying land taken from them; the Gemara says this law does not apply in Babylonia.
The tax paid to the government on land.

gittin-60b-13-14.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi wants to study with Abaye, but Abaye is busy irrigating his fields. Rav Shimi offers to irrigate by day so they can learn at night. He then tells the upper-field owners that the lower fields drink first (Rav's view) and the lower-field owners the opposite (Shmuel's view), and while they argue he dams the river and waters Abaye's fields. Abaye points out he acted on two opposing opinions, and refused to eat that year's produce, fearing the water came unlawfully.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the Sage whose fields needed water

people.name: Rav
people.about: cited for one view on who drinks first

gittin-60b-15-15.note: Residents of Bei Harmakh dug a channel to circle the river's water around their fields and then return it downstream. Owners of fields upstream complained to Abaye that the river no longer flowed as before. Abaye first suggested digging a little deeper, but the upstream owners said that would dry their own pits. Abaye then ordered the residents to remove themselves from there and dam the diversion they had made.

gittin-61a-3-3.note: Rav Kahana, walking to Huzal, saw a man knocking dates from a palm tree with sticks, and he gathered and ate some. The man said that since he had thrown them down with his own hand, they were legally his. Rav Kahana replied that the man must come from the city of Rabbi Yoshiya, so he knows halakha (Jewish law), and quoted a verse that a righteous person is a foundation of the world. The text does not say what happened to the dates afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: described in the text as a great Sage of Huzal

terms.meaning: Jewish law.

gittin-62a-13-15.note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda debate whether to stand for the passing Geneiva, one saying he is a son of Torah, the other calling him argumentative. Geneiva greets them first, with 'peace' twice, calling them kings, and backs this up with verses showing Sages are called kings and that kings get a doubled greeting. When they offer him food, he declines, citing Rav's teaching that one must feed one's animal before eating, and he has not yet fed his.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: quoted as saying in Rav's name that animals are fed first

terms.meaning: peace; the standard greeting.

gittin-63b-11-14.note: A husband's agent found the wife kneading dough, and she said her hands were messy, so he should hold the divorce document for her. Rav Nahman thought the divorce takes effect if the law follows Rabbi Hanina. Rava objected that by appointing the agent as her own agent before he delivered it, she cancelled his role for the husband, so the divorce does not take effect. Rabbi Ami agreed with Rava, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba finally said the question was uncertain to him too.

terms.meaning: the document a husband gives to end a marriage.
someone appointed to carry out an act, such as delivering a divorce document, for another person.

gittin-63b-17-17.note: A husband told witnesses to write and sign a divorce document for his wife Nefata, but they mistakenly wrote the name Tefata. Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta, in Rav's name, rules that the document is invalid because the name is wrong. The witnesses also cannot write a corrected one, because they already carried out their task as the husband's agents and are no longer his agents.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta

terms.meaning: the document a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-65b-15-15.note: Geneiva, being led out to execution, said to give 400 dinars' worth of his wine to Rabbi Avina. Rabbi Zeira says Avina should go to his teacher Rav Huna, because his claim depends on Rav Huna's view. Rav Huna says a deathbed gift can be taken back if the giver recovers, and the same applies to a divorce document given on a deathbed.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rabbi Avina's teacher, per the text

terms.meaning: A coin used as a unit of money.
The document (a get) a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-66a-14-15.note: A man found a schoolteacher, the teacher's son and a third person in the synagogue, and told 'two of you' to write a divorce document for his wife. The teacher then died, so the question was whether the son and the third person still count as the two agents. Rav Nahman said people do not appoint a son as agent in his father's presence, while Rav Pappi said they do, and Rava ruled that they do.

terms.meaning: the document a husband gives to end a marriage.
someone appointed to act for another person, here to write and deliver the divorce document.

gittin-66a-11-11.note: A healthy man said 'Write a bill of divorce for my wife,' then climbed to a roof, fell and died. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if he fell on purpose, taking his own life, the bill is valid, since he clearly meant to give it. If the wind made him fall, the bill is not valid, because there was no clear intent to give it to her.

terms.meaning: the early collection of Jewish law that the Talmud's discussion is built around.
the document a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-67a-5-6.note: Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled like Rabbi Yosei, that verbal instructions cannot be passed on through an agent. His son Rabbi Shimon asked why, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Hanina of Ono disagree with Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him to be silent, saying that if he had seen Rabbi Yosei he would know that his reasoning goes along with his statements, which is why he finds Yosei's opinion most reliable.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; here, which opinion is the accepted ruling.

gittin-67b-15-16.note: The Exilarch's household would make the pious Rav Amram sleep on snow, then ask what food he wanted. Expecting them to do the opposite of whatever he said, he asked for red meat and diluted wine. They brought fatty meat and undiluted wine instead, which is what he had wanted, because that is the cure for the chills. Yalta, Rav Nahman's wife, heard he was suffering and put him in the bathhouse water until it turned red like blood. His skin was left covered with spots that looked like coins.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia; his household mistreated Rav Amram

terms.meaning: the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

gittin-67b-18-21.note: The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet why he will not eat with them. Rav Sheshet proves the servants are untrustworthy about meat: a stolen leg is replaced by one cut from a live animal. They later plant a bone in his meat and dig a hidden pit for blind Rav Sheshet, but he avoids both, and a signal from Rav Chisda and a child's verse also help him. Rav Sheshet says he suspected them anyway.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
A limb cut from a living animal, which the Torah forbids eating.

gittin-69b-6-6.note: The passage gives a folk remedy for intestinal pain: drink one hundred long peppers a day in wine, from a set of three hundred. It then reports that Ravin of Neresh prepared one hundred and fifty Babylonian peppers for Rav Ashi's daughter, who had this illness, and she was healed.

gittin-69b-11-11.note: This is a second remedy for the same illness: roast a fish in a blacksmith's house, eat it with the water used to cool red-hot metal, and drink that water. As supporting evidence, the Gemara tells of a goat that drank such water, and when it was slaughtered, no spleen was found inside it.

terms.meaning: the Talmud's long discussion that explains and expands on the Mishna.

gittin-70a-1-1.note: The passage gives a remedy for a skin condition: roast seven large wheat kernels on the blade of a new hoe, extract the oil and rub it on the skin. It reports that Rav Shimi bar Ashi used this on a gentile whose condition was actually leprosy, and he was healed.

terms.meaning: a non-Jew.

gittin-70a-22-22.note: Abaye says that if a person does these actions in the given order he will die, and out of order he will only become weak. The Gemara objects that a woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of these actions and he died. It answers that the slave was weak, and an ordinary person would die only by doing all of them in order.

people.name: Me'oret
people.about: a woman who made her slave do these actions

gittin-72a-17-18.note: When Rabba bar Avuh is ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nachman visit him. Rav Huna has Rav Nachman ask whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei, and Rabba bar Avuh says yes, in Rav's name. Rav Huna then gives Rabbi Yosei's reason: the date on a document shows when it takes effect. The Gemara concludes Rav Huna was unsure whether this applies when the husband stated a condition as he handed over the divorce document.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.

gittin-73a-9-14.note: A man sold land and took responsibility for any unavoidable accident to it. Later the government diverted a river through the land. Ravina first told the seller to pay the buyer, but Rav Aha bar Tahalifa and then Rava said this was an uncommon accident not covered. Ravina objected from a teaching about conditional divorces. Rava showed the teaching contradicts itself, and Ravina agreed that it cannot be relied on and that reason says an uncommon accident is not covered.

terms.meaning: an early Jewish teaching that is not in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.
damage no one could prevent, which the seller here agreed to pay for.

gittin-73a-15-17.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, bought sesame on the bank of the Malka River and hired sailors to carry it across, with the sailors accepting responsibility for any unavoidable accident. The river was then dammed, and the two Sages demanded that the sailors hire donkeys to carry the sesame instead. In court, Rava scolded them as "white geese who strip men of their cloaks." He ruled that a dammed river is an uncommon accident that the sailors had not taken responsibility for.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua

terms.meaning: damage no one could prevent, which the sailors agreed to pay for.

gittin-74a-7-7.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel tells of an incident in Tzaidan. A man told his wife the divorce document was valid on condition that she give him back his coat, but she had lost it. The Rabbis ruled that she must give him the coat's value, which fulfills the condition, and she is then divorced.

terms.meaning: the document a husband gives to end a marriage.
a requirement attached to a divorce, which must be met for the divorce to take effect.

gittin-74b-11-12.note: A landowner offered his sharecropper one third of the crop instead of the usual quarter, if the sharecropper watered the field four times instead of the usual three. Rain came, so the fourth watering was not needed. Rav Yosef said the condition was not fulfilled, so he gets only a quarter. Rabba said the rain helped the sharecropper, so he should still get one third. The passage gives both views and no final ruling.

terms.meaning: a worker who farms someone else's field and is paid with a share of the crop.

gittin-77a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught that if a man says a divorce is valid if he does not return after the pilgrimage Festival, it takes effect only thirty days after the festival. Rabbi Hiyya taught this publicly in the name of Yehuda HaNasi, and people praised it, but when he taught it as a majority opinion, they did not. The Gemara concludes that the law does not follow this ruling, so the Sages did not want it accepted as law.

terms.meaning: an early Jewish teaching that is not in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.
Jewish law; here, the accepted ruling.

gittin-77b-5-8.note: A dying man wrote a divorce document for his wife but could not give it to her. Rava told those who asked to have him transfer to her the place where the document lay, so that she could take possession by closing and opening the door. Rav Ilish objected that whatever a wife acquires belongs to her husband, and Rava was embarrassed. It then turned out she was only betrothed, and Rava said his ruling had been right, since a betrothed woman's acquisitions are not her husband's. He then concluded that it makes no difference whether she is betrothed or married, because the divorce document and the courtyard come into her possession at the same moment.

terms.meaning: engaged under Jewish law, which is a legal step before full marriage.
the document a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-77b-15-15.note: A man threw a divorce document to his wife while she stood in a courtyard, and it landed on a wooden board. Rav Yosef said to check the board's size. If it covers four cubits by four cubits, it counts as a separate domain and she is not divorced. If it is smaller, it is part of the courtyard and she is divorced.

terms.meaning: an ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.
a legally distinct area; whether the document lands in her domain decides if the divorce takes effect.

gittin-83a-3-10.note: After Rabbi Eliezer died, four Sages (Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva) argued against his view that a husband may give a divorce on the condition that his ex-wife not marry one particular man. Each gave a reason that such a divorce is not a true 'severance,' meaning a clean break. Rabbi Yehoshua then told them that even though their objections are valid, one does not refute the opinion of a 'lion' after his death, since he might have answered had he been alive.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: the Sage whose ruling was challenged after his death

terms.meaning: the Torah's rule that a childless widow may marry her late husband's brother.
a child born from certain forbidden relationships, who faces restrictions on marriage.
the Torah's phrase for a divorce document, meaning it fully cuts the marriage bond.

gittin-89a-17-17.note: A rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a Torah student. Rav Hama asked her father what happened, and he said the student had betrothed her on a condition (that he not go to Bei Hozai), which he broke by going there, cancelling the betrothal. Rav Hama replied that this explanation did not exist when the rumor began, so the father cannot create it now, and the rumor must be treated strictly.

terms.meaning: the legal first step of marriage in Jewish law, which is binding and can only be ended by divorce.

gittin-89a-18-18.note: A rumor spread that a woman was betrothed with a mat of dates. Rav Idi bar Avin asked Abaye whether to suppress the rumor. Abaye ruled that it should be suppressed, even by the view that rumors usually are not. If she marries someone else, people would not slander her, since they would conclude that the Sages checked and found the mat was worth less than a peruta, so the betrothal was invalid.

terms.meaning: the smallest coin in use, the minimum value needed for a valid betrothal.
the legal first step of marriage in Jewish law.

gittin-89a-19-19.note: A rumor spreads that a woman was engaged to one of the sons of a certain man, who had both adult and minor sons, and nobody knows which son. Rava says that even those who normally say a rumor should be left alone would agree to suppress this one. Otherwise people might slander her; instead they will say the Sages checked and it was an engagement of a minor.

terms.meaning: A formal engagement that, in Jewish law, already binds the couple until divorce.

gittin-89b-1-1.note: A rumor spread that a woman was betrothed to a minor boy who looked like an adult. Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a precedent where the Sages said not to worry that people would think she was betrothed, because the boy had not reached adult understanding, citing a verse about the 'divisions of Reuben.' So the betrothal counts as entirely invalid and there is no concern of slander.

terms.meaning: a child below the legal age of adulthood, whose betrothal has no legal effect.
